short: How many rupees of sales a company earns for every rupee invested in its factories, machines and other long-term physical assets.
kid: You buy one oven for your cookie stall. If that one oven helps you bake and sell lots of cookies, it is working hard for you.
detail: Fixed asset turnover divides revenue by net fixed assets, meaning property, plant and equipment after depreciation, usually averaged over the year. It shows how productively a company uses its plant and machinery to generate sales. Capital-heavy businesses such as steel, cement, power and telecom typically show low ratios, often around 1-2x or even lower, while retailers, IT services firms and FMCG companies run far higher. A rising ratio can signal better capacity utilisation; a falling one may mean fresh capacity has been added but not yet filled, which is common right after a big capex cycle. Common confusion: a very high ratio is not automatically good, because it can simply reflect old, heavily depreciated assets or leased assets that sit outside the fixed-asset line. Compare within the same industry and over several years, not across sectors.
example: Say ABC Ltd reports revenue of ₹1,200 crore and average net fixed assets of ₹400 crore. Its fixed asset turnover ratio is 1,200 / 400 = 3x, meaning every rupee of plant and machinery supports ₹3 of sales.
formula: Fixed asset turnover = Revenue / Average net fixed assets

short: How many rupees of sales a company generates for every rupee tied up in its day-to-day working capital (current assets minus current liabilities).
kid: To run a lemonade stand you keep some lemons, sugar and cups ready. This checks how much lemonade you sell for all the stuff you keep ready.
detail: Working capital turnover divides revenue by average net working capital, which is current assets such as inventory, receivables and cash minus current liabilities such as payables and short-term dues. It shows how efficiently a business converts the money locked in its operating cycle into sales. A higher ratio generally means the company needs less working capital to grow, freeing cash for capex, dividends or debt reduction. Several large Indian FMCG companies run negative working capital because they collect from distributors quickly and pay suppliers later, which makes the ratio negative or meaningless. Common confusion: an extremely high ratio can be a warning sign rather than a strength, because working capital may be too thin to absorb a shock. Analysts often exclude cash and short-term debt to focus on operating items, and read the ratio alongside the cash conversion cycle.
example: Say ABC Ltd has annual revenue of ₹600 crore and average net working capital of ₹75 crore. Its working capital turnover is 600 / 75 = 8x, so each rupee of working capital supports ₹8 of sales.
formula: Working capital turnover = Revenue / Average net working capital

short: How many times a company sells through and replaces its stock of goods during a year.
kid: A toy shop fills its shelves, sells all the toys, then fills them again. Counting how many times the shelves get emptied in a year tells you how fast toys sell.
detail: Inventory turnover measures how many times a company sells and replenishes its inventory in a period, usually computed as cost of goods sold divided by average inventory. Using cost of goods sold rather than revenue keeps both numbers at cost, though some data providers use revenue, so check the method before comparing. High turnover suggests strong demand, lean stock management and less risk of goods becoming obsolete; low turnover can point to weak sales, overstocking or slow-moving items. Norms vary hugely: a supermarket chain may turn its inventory 10 or more times a year, while a jeweller or heavy-equipment maker may turn it only 2 or 3 times. Common confusion: very high turnover is not always good if it causes stock-outs and lost sales. Dividing 365 by this ratio gives days inventory outstanding.
example: Say ABC Ltd has cost of goods sold of ₹480 crore and average inventory of ₹60 crore. Inventory turnover is 480 / 60 = 8 times a year, which works out to about 365 / 8 = 45.6 days of inventory.
formula: Inventory turnover = Cost of goods sold / Average inventory

short: The average number of days a company holds its stock of goods before selling it.
kid: Think of sweets sitting in a jar at a shop. This counts how many days, on average, a sweet waits in the jar before someone buys it.
detail: Days inventory outstanding (DIO) converts inventory turnover into days: it tells you how long, on average, raw materials, work in progress and finished goods sit with a company before being sold. It is usually calculated as average inventory divided by cost of goods sold, multiplied by 365, though some analysts use 360. Lower DIO means cash is freed up faster and there is less risk of obsolescence, which matters for fashion, electronics and pharma. Higher DIO can be deliberate, for example when a company stockpiles raw materials ahead of a price rise, or when an Indian consumer company builds stock before the festive season. DIO is one of the three building blocks of the cash conversion cycle, along with DSO and DPO. Common confusion: compare DIO only within the same industry and at the same point in the year, since seasonality distorts year-end figures.
example: Say ABC Ltd holds average inventory of ₹50 crore and has annual cost of goods sold of ₹365 crore. Its DIO is (50 / 365) x 365 = 50 days, so goods sit for about 50 days before being sold.
formula: DIO = (Average inventory / Cost of goods sold) x 365

short: How many times in a year a company collects the money its customers owe it for goods sold on credit.
kid: Sometimes friends take a lemonade now and pay you later. This counts how quickly and how often those friends pay you back.
detail: Receivables turnover divides credit sales, in practice often total revenue, by average trade receivables, the amounts customers owe. A higher ratio means the company collects faster, carries less risk of bad debts and needs less working capital. A falling ratio can be an early warning that customers are struggling, that sales teams are offering looser credit to push volumes, or, in worse cases, that revenue is being booked aggressively. In India, receivables are closely watched in sectors that sell to governments and state utilities, such as power, infrastructure and defence, where payments can be delayed for long periods. Common confusion: the ratio is a count of collection cycles, not a number of days; divide 365 by it to get days sales outstanding. Also make sure receivables are measured consistently, either gross or net of provisions for doubtful debts, across years and companies.
example: Say ABC Ltd has annual credit sales of ₹900 crore and average receivables of ₹150 crore. Receivables turnover is 900 / 150 = 6 times, which equals about 365 / 6 = 60.8 days to collect.
formula: Receivables turnover = Net credit sales / Average trade receivables

short: The average number of days a company takes to collect payment from customers after making a sale on credit.
kid: You give your friend a toy car today and they promise to pay you later. This counts how many days you usually wait until they pay.
detail: Days sales outstanding (DSO) measures the average collection period: how many days of sales are sitting with customers as unpaid bills. It is calculated as average trade receivables divided by revenue, ideally credit revenue, multiplied by 365. Lower DSO means faster cash collection and a lighter working capital burden. Large Indian IT services companies report DSO with their quarterly results, and analysts watch it closely because a jump can mean clients are paying slowly. Rising DSO while revenue is growing fast can be a red flag that sales are being pushed on generous credit terms or recognised too early. Common confusion: DSO depends on the industry's normal credit terms, so 90 days may be routine for a capital-goods maker and alarming for a consumer brand. For a single quarter, use the quarter's revenue with about 91 days, or annualise revenue first.
example: Say ABC Ltd has average receivables of ₹120 crore and annual revenue of ₹730 crore. DSO = (120 / 730) x 365 = 60 days, so customers take about two months to pay.
formula: DSO = (Average trade receivables / Revenue) x 365

short: How many times in a year a company pays off what it owes its suppliers for goods and services bought on credit.
kid: Your lemonade stand gets lemons from a neighbour and pays her later. This counts how often you pay her back in a year.
detail: Payables turnover divides purchases on credit, often approximated by cost of goods sold, by average trade payables, the amounts owed to suppliers. A lower ratio means the company takes longer to pay, effectively using supplier credit as free short-term funding; a higher ratio means it pays quickly. Large companies with bargaining power, such as big retailers or automakers, often stretch payables, while smaller firms may be forced to pay fast. Neither extreme is ideal: paying too slowly can damage supplier relationships, attract interest penalties or signal cash stress. In India, under the rules as of 2025, the MSMED Act requires buyers to pay micro and small enterprises within 45 days at most, and income-tax law allows the deduction for late-paid dues only when actually paid. Common confusion: dividing 365 by this ratio gives days payable outstanding, which is a number of days rather than a count of payment cycles.
example: Say ABC Ltd has annual purchases of ₹500 crore and average trade payables of ₹100 crore. Payables turnover is 500 / 100 = 5 times, meaning it settles supplier bills roughly every 365 / 5 = 73 days.
formula: Payables turnover = Credit purchases (or Cost of goods sold) / Average trade payables

short: The average number of days a company takes to pay its suppliers after receiving goods or services on credit.
kid: Your shop gets sweets from a big sweet-maker and pays later. This counts how many days you usually wait before paying the sweet-maker.
detail: Days payable outstanding (DPO) measures how long a company takes, on average, to pay its suppliers. It is calculated as average trade payables divided by cost of goods sold or purchases, multiplied by 365. A higher DPO means the company holds on to cash longer, using suppliers as an interest-free source of funding, which shortens the cash conversion cycle. Companies with strong bargaining power, such as large retailers and e-commerce platforms, often run high DPO. But a sudden jump can signal cash trouble rather than strength, especially if it comes with rising short-term borrowing or supplier complaints. Watch also for supply chain finance arrangements, where a bank pays suppliers early and the company repays the bank later, which can make DPO look healthier than the true position. In India, payments to micro and small suppliers face statutory time limits under the rules as of 2025.
example: Say ABC Ltd has average trade payables of ₹80 crore and annual cost of goods sold of ₹584 crore. DPO = (80 / 584) x 365 = 50 days, so it pays suppliers about 50 days after buying.
formula: DPO = (Average trade payables / Cost of goods sold) x 365

short: The number of days between a company paying for its raw materials and collecting cash from customers for the finished goods.
kid: You spend your pocket money on lemons, make lemonade, sell it and get money back. This counts the days your pocket money is away before it comes home.
detail: The cash conversion cycle (CCC) measures how many days a company's cash is tied up in operations. It equals days inventory outstanding plus days sales outstanding minus days payable outstanding. The first two capture how long goods sit unsold and how long customers take to pay; subtracting DPO credits the company for the time suppliers let it defer payment. A shorter cycle means the business needs less working capital and can grow with less outside funding. A negative CCC, seen at Amazon for much of its history and at some large Indian FMCG companies, means customers pay before suppliers are paid, so growth actually releases cash. Common confusion: CCC is not the same as the operating cycle, which ignores payables. A falling CCC driven only by stretching suppliers is lower quality than one driven by faster inventory movement or quicker collections.
example: Say ABC Ltd has DIO of 60 days, DSO of 45 days and DPO of 40 days. Its cash conversion cycle is 60 + 45 - 40 = 65 days.
formula: CCC = Days inventory outstanding + Days sales outstanding - Days payable outstanding

short: The number of days from buying stock to collecting cash from customers after selling it.
kid: You buy apples, wait for them to be sold at your stall, then wait for the buyer to pay. The whole wait, from buying to getting paid, is the cycle.
detail: The operating cycle is the total time from acquiring inventory to receiving cash from its sale. It equals days inventory outstanding plus days sales outstanding. It captures the full length of a company's core business loop: buying or making goods, holding them, selling them on credit and collecting payment. A long operating cycle, typical of real estate developers, shipbuilders, capital-goods makers and jewellers, means large amounts of funding are needed to keep the business running. A short cycle, typical of supermarkets and restaurants, means cash comes back quickly. Accounting standards, including Ind AS, also use the operating cycle to classify assets and liabilities as current or non-current, which is why a property developer can show flats that take years to sell as current inventory. Common confusion: the operating cycle does not subtract payables; doing so gives the cash conversion cycle, also called the net operating cycle.
example: Say ABC Ltd holds inventory for 70 days and takes 50 days to collect from customers. Its operating cycle is 70 + 50 = 120 days; if it pays suppliers in 40 days, its cash conversion cycle is 120 - 40 = 80 days.
formula: Operating cycle = Days inventory outstanding + Days sales outstanding

short: The share of a company's EBITDA (profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation) that actually turns into operating cash in the same period.
kid: Your notebook says you earned ten coins at the stall, but some friends have not paid yet. This checks how many coins actually reached your piggy bank.
detail: The cash conversion ratio compares cash flow from operations (CFO or OCF) with EBITDA, showing how much of reported operating profit is backed by real cash. Because EBITDA is an accounting measure, it can be flattered by aggressive revenue recognition, rising receivables or inventory build-up; operating cash flow is much harder to dress up. Since CFO is after tax and after working-capital changes, even well-run companies rarely convert 100% every year, so analysts look at the average over several years rather than a single period. A persistently low ratio, with profits rising but cash lagging, is a classic red flag that forensic accounting analysts look for in Indian and global companies alike. Common confusion: some analysts define cash conversion differently, for example as free cash flow divided by net profit, so always check which version a report uses before comparing numbers.
example: Say ABC Ltd reports EBITDA of ₹250 crore and cash flow from operations of ₹200 crore. Its cash conversion ratio is 200 / 250 = 80%, so four-fifths of its operating profit arrived as cash.
formula: Cash conversion ratio = Cash flow from operations / EBITDA

short: A company's net worth according to its balance sheet (assets minus liabilities) divided by the number of shares outstanding.
kid: If a toy box holds toys worth ten coins and five friends own it together, each friend's part is worth two coins.
detail: Book value per share (BVPS) is shareholders' equity divided by the number of equity shares outstanding. It represents the accounting value attributable to each share if the company sold its assets at balance-sheet values and paid off all liabilities. Investors compare it with the market price through the price-to-book (P/B) ratio, which is used especially for banks, NBFCs and insurers, whose assets are mostly financial and closer to fair value. For asset-light businesses like IT services or consumer brands, BVPS says little, because brands, people and customer relationships are largely absent from the balance sheet. Common confusion: book value is not liquidation value or intrinsic value; assets may be worth much more or less than their recorded amounts. Preference capital is excluded, and for banks analysts often use adjusted book value after deducting net NPAs, the bad loans not yet provided for.
example: Say ABC Ltd has shareholders' equity of ₹1,500 crore and 30 crore shares outstanding. BVPS = 1,500 / 30 = ₹50; if the share trades at ₹100, the price-to-book ratio is 100 / 50 = 2x.
formula: BVPS = (Shareholders' equity - Preference equity) / Number of equity shares outstanding

short: The percentage of a company's profit that it pays out to shareholders as dividends rather than keeping in the business.
kid: You earn ten sweets at your stall. If you share four with your friends and keep six to grow your stall, you shared four out of ten.
detail: The dividend payout ratio is the share of net profit distributed to shareholders as dividends, calculated as total dividends divided by net profit, or dividend per share divided by earnings per share. Mature, cash-rich companies with limited reinvestment needs, such as many PSUs and some IT, tobacco and FMCG companies in India, tend to have high payout ratios, while fast-growing companies usually pay little and reinvest instead. Its mirror image is the retention ratio; the two add up to 100%. A payout ratio above 100% means the company is paying out more than it earned, drawing on reserves or borrowing, which is rarely sustainable. Common confusion: the payout ratio relates dividends to profit, while dividend yield relates dividends to the share price. Buybacks are a second way to return cash and are excluded from the basic ratio, so the total cash returned to shareholders can be higher.
example: Say ABC Ltd earns a net profit of ₹400 crore and declares dividends totalling ₹120 crore. Its dividend payout ratio is 120 / 400 = 30%, and its retention ratio is 100% - 30% = 70%.
formula: Dividend payout ratio = Dividends / Net profit = Dividend per share / Earnings per share

short: The percentage of a company's profit that it keeps and reinvests in the business instead of paying out as dividends.
kid: You earn ten coins at your lemonade stand. If you save six to buy a bigger table for the stall, you kept six out of ten to help it grow.
detail: The retention ratio, also called the plowback ratio, is the portion of net profit a company keeps rather than distributing as dividends. It equals 1 minus the dividend payout ratio. Retained earnings fund new plants, research or acquisitions without fresh capital. The retention ratio is a key input in the sustainable growth rate, which multiplies it by return on equity to estimate how fast a company can grow on its own resources. A high retention ratio is only valuable if the company earns good returns on the reinvested money; retaining profits and investing them at returns below the cost of equity destroys value. Common confusion: retained earnings on the balance sheet are a cumulative total built over many years, while the retention ratio is a single-period percentage. In insurance, the term retention ratio means something different: the share of premium an insurer keeps rather than passing to reinsurers.
example: Say ABC Ltd earns ₹500 crore and pays ₹150 crore in dividends. Its retention ratio is (500 - 150) / 500 = 70%, so ₹350 crore stays in the business.
formula: Retention ratio = 1 - Dividend payout ratio = (Net profit - Dividends) / Net profit

short: The yearly dividend a share pays, shown as a percentage of the share's current market price.
kid: You buy a hen for ten coins and she gives you eggs worth one coin every year. The eggs are like a small thank-you gift for owning the hen.
detail: Dividend yield is annual dividends per share divided by the current share price. It shows the cash income a stock pays relative to its price today, and is often compared with fixed deposit rates. Because the price is in the denominator, yield rises when a share price falls, so a very high yield can be a warning that the market expects the dividend to be cut, a situation called a yield trap. Indian PSUs in sectors like coal, oil and power have often been among the higher-yielding stocks. The standard figure uses dividends paid over the trailing twelve months; forward yield uses expected dividends. Common confusion: dividend yield is not the same as total return, which also includes price change. In India, dividends are taxed in the hands of shareholders at their slab rates under the rules as of 2025, which affects post-tax yield.
example: Say a share of ABC Ltd trades at ₹400 and paid total dividends of ₹12 over the last year. Its dividend yield is 12 / 400 = 3%; if the price falls to ₹300 with the same dividend, the yield rises to 12 / 300 = 4%.
formula: Dividend yield = Annual dividend per share / Current share price

short: The fastest a company can grow using only the profits it keeps, without issuing new shares or increasing its borrowing relative to its size.
kid: If your lemonade stand keeps some of its coins to buy more lemons each week, it can grow a little bigger every week all by itself, without asking anyone for help.
detail: The sustainable growth rate (SGR) is the maximum rate at which a company can grow revenue and assets while keeping its debt-to-equity ratio and dividend policy unchanged, funding growth only from retained earnings. It is calculated as return on equity multiplied by the retention ratio. The logic: equity grows only by the profits kept in the business, and if leverage stays constant, assets and sales can grow at the same pace. A company growing faster than its SGR must borrow more, issue shares, cut dividends or improve margins and asset efficiency, which is why fast-growing Indian banks and NBFCs regularly raise fresh equity. Growing below SGR tends to build up surplus cash. Common confusion: SGR is not a forecast of actual growth; it is a self-funding ceiling. It also assumes ROE stays stable, which rarely holds exactly, and textbooks differ on using opening or average equity.
example: Say ABC Ltd earns a return on equity of 20% and retains 60% of its profit. Its sustainable growth rate is 20% x 0.60 = 12% a year.
formula: SGR = Return on equity x Retention ratio

short: The share of a company's pre-tax profit that it actually pays or books as tax, after all deductions, exemptions and credits.
kid: The rule says you share three of every ten sweets with the class jar, but some days you get to share fewer. The number you really share is what counts here.
detail: The effective tax rate is a company's total tax expense, current plus deferred, divided by its profit before tax as shown in the profit and loss statement. It often differs from the statutory corporate tax rate because of tax holidays, SEZ benefits, R&D deductions, losses carried forward, income taxed at different rates, foreign operations and non-deductible expenses. In India, many companies have opted for the concessional regime introduced in 2019, which brought the statutory rate for domestic companies to about 25% including surcharge and cess, under the rules as of 2025. Analysts track the ETR because a falling rate can flatter net profit without any improvement in operations, and an expiring tax holiday can cut future earnings. Common confusion: the ETR uses tax expense, which includes deferred tax, while the cash tax rate uses taxes actually paid.
example: Say ABC Ltd reports profit before tax of ₹800 crore and total tax expense of ₹184 crore. Its effective tax rate is 184 / 800 = 23%, below the statutory rate thanks to, say, a tax holiday on one plant.
formula: Effective tax rate = Total tax expense / Profit before tax

short: The steady yearly growth rate that would take a value from its starting level to its ending level over several years.
kid: Your plant grew fast one year and slowly the next. This pretends it grew at one steady speed every year, so you can compare it with other plants.
detail: Compound annual growth rate (CAGR) is the constant annual rate at which a value would have grown from its beginning level to its ending level, assuming growth compounded every year. It smooths volatile year-to-year changes into a single comparable number, which is why it is used everywhere: company revenue and profit growth, mutual fund returns, index performance and sector forecasts. In India, mutual fund factsheets show returns for periods longer than one year as CAGR. Common confusion: CAGR is not the simple average of annual growth rates, which overstates growth when returns swing; nor does it describe the path taken, so two investments with the same CAGR can carry very different risk. It also ignores money added or withdrawn along the way, for which XIRR is the right tool. Be careful with start and end points, since picking a crash year as the base can make CAGR look spectacular.
example: Say ABC Ltd's revenue grew from ₹100 crore to ₹200 crore over 5 years. Its CAGR is (200 / 100)^(1/5) - 1 = about 14.9% a year, not the simple 100% / 5 = 20%.
formula: CAGR = (Ending value / Beginning value)^(1 / Number of years) - 1

short: The percentage change in a figure compared with the same period one year earlier.
kid: Last birthday you were this tall, and this birthday you are taller. Comparing birthday to birthday shows how much you grew in a whole year.
detail: Year-on-year (YoY) growth compares a figure, such as revenue, profit, sales volume or inflation, with the same period a year earlier: this quarter against the same quarter last year, or this month against the same month last year. Because it compares like seasons with like, YoY removes most seasonal effects, which matters a lot in India, where festive quarters, monsoon timing and financial-year-end pushes skew results. That is why quarterly results headlines and official inflation and GDP data usually lead with YoY numbers. Common confusion: YoY says nothing about the most recent direction; a company can show strong YoY growth while its sales are falling quarter-on-quarter. A weak base period, such as a pandemic-hit year, can produce inflated YoY figures, known as the base effect. For multi-year comparisons, use CAGR instead of averaging several YoY rates.
example: Say ABC Ltd's revenue was ₹500 crore in the July-September quarter last year and ₹575 crore in the same quarter this year. YoY growth is (575 - 500) / 500 = 15%.
formula: YoY growth = (Current period value - Same period last year) / Same period last year x 100

short: The percentage change in a figure compared with the immediately preceding quarter.
kid: Count your marbles at the end of every three months. This compares today's count with the last count, just three months ago.
detail: Quarter-on-quarter (QoQ) growth, also called sequential growth, compares a figure with the immediately preceding three-month period, such as July-September against April-June. It captures the latest momentum faster than year-on-year growth, which is why Indian IT services companies, banks and analysts highlight sequential growth in revenue, deposits and loan books. Its weakness is seasonality: a retailer's festive quarter will almost always beat the quarter before, and many Indian companies see their January-March quarter boosted by year-end billing. So QoQ is most meaningful for businesses with little seasonality, or when read alongside YoY figures. Common confusion: QoQ growth is not an annual rate; 3% QoQ compounds to roughly 12.6% over four quarters, not 12%. US GDP growth is usually reported as a seasonally adjusted annualised rate, which is different from a raw QoQ change.
example: Say ABC Ltd earned revenue of ₹400 crore in April-June and ₹420 crore in July-September. QoQ growth is (420 - 400) / 400 = 5%.
formula: QoQ growth = (Current quarter value - Previous quarter value) / Previous quarter value x 100

short: A company's figures for the most recent twelve months, regardless of where its financial year starts or ends.
kid: Instead of waiting for your birthday to count a year, you look back twelve months from today. That way your count is always fresh.
detail: Trailing twelve months (TTM), also called last twelve months (LTM), refers to a company's financial data for the latest four reported quarters combined. It gives the most up-to-date annual view without waiting for the full financial year to end. For example, after a company reports its September quarter, TTM figures cover October of the previous year through September. Screeners and market data sites use TTM earnings to calculate the trailing P/E ratio, and dealmakers use TTM revenue or EBITDA for valuation multiples. A simple way to compute it: last full-year figure, plus year-to-date figures for the current year, minus the same year-to-date period of the previous year. Common confusion: TTM is backward-looking and differs from forward or estimated numbers, so a trailing P/E and a forward P/E for the same stock can differ sharply. One-off items in the last four quarters can also distort TTM figures.
example: Say ABC Ltd earned ₹100 crore in FY25, and its April-September profit was ₹60 crore in FY26 versus ₹45 crore in the same half of FY25. Its TTM profit is 100 + 60 - 45 = ₹115 crore.
formula: TTM = Last full financial year + Current year-to-date - Prior year's same year-to-date period

short: A projection of full-year results made by stretching a recent period's performance, such as one month or quarter, across a whole year.
kid: If your lemonade stand sells ten cups this week, you can guess how many cups you might sell in a whole year if every week is like this one.
detail: Run rate annualises a recent short-period figure, usually revenue, by multiplying a month by 12 or a quarter by 4. Startups and SaaS companies often quote annualised revenue run rate to show their current scale, especially when growing fast, since last year's numbers understate their present size. Indian companies also refer to a run rate for monthly sales, order inflow or capex. It is useful as a quick snapshot of current momentum, but it assumes the recent period repeats exactly, ignoring seasonality, one-off contracts, customer losses and pricing changes. A festive-quarter run rate for a retailer, for instance, would overstate annual sales. Common confusion: run rate is a projection, not reported revenue, and it is not the same as annual recurring revenue (ARR), which counts only contracted recurring subscriptions. Treat startup claims based on a single exceptional month with caution.
example: Say a hypothetical startup, XYZ Pvt Ltd, books ₹5 crore of revenue in March. Its annualised revenue run rate is ₹5 crore x 12 = ₹60 crore, even if its actual revenue for the full year was only ₹40 crore.
formula: Annualised run rate = Revenue for the period x (12 / Number of months in the period)

short: Sales growth from stores open for a set period, usually a year or more, so newly opened stores do not inflate the figure.
kid: If your ice cream shop opens a second shop, of course you sell more. This only looks at your first shop, to see if it is really selling more than before.
detail: Same-store sales growth (SSSG) measures the revenue change at stores that have been operating for a defined period, commonly 12 months or more, excluding stores opened or closed in between. It separates organic demand from growth bought through expansion, so it is one of the most watched metrics for retailers, quick-service restaurant chains, jewellers and apparel brands in India. Strong SSSG means existing outlets are attracting more customers, selling more per visit or raising prices; weak SSSG with strong total growth suggests the company is relying on new openings, which need constant capital. Analysts often split SSSG into change in footfall or order count and change in average bill size. Common confusion: there is no single standard definition; companies choose their own cut-off period and treatment of renovated or relocated stores, so compare SSSG across firms with care. Comparable sales and like-for-like sales are the same idea under different names.
example: Say ABC Retail Ltd's 100 stores, all open for over a year, grew sales from ₹1,000 crore to ₹1,080 crore, and 20 new stores added another ₹120 crore. SSSG is (1,080 - 1,000) / 1,000 = 8%, while total sales growth is (1,200 - 1,000) / 1,000 = 20%.
formula: SSSG = (Current period sales of comparable stores - Prior period sales of the same stores) / Prior period sales of the same stores x 100

short: Financial statements where every line is shown as a percentage of one base figure, such as revenue or total assets.
kid: Instead of saying you spent five coins on sweets, you say you spent half of all your coins on sweets. Then big and small piggy banks are easy to compare.
detail: Common-size statements express each item in a financial statement as a percentage of a single base: revenue for the profit and loss statement, and total assets, or total liabilities and equity, for the balance sheet. This is also called vertical analysis, because you read down a single period's column. Converting rupee amounts into percentages lets you compare companies of very different sizes, for example a small-cap and a large-cap FMCG company, and spot shifts in cost structure over time, such as raw material costs rising from 45% to 52% of sales. It also makes margins visible at every level, from gross margin to net margin. Common confusion: vertical analysis compares items within one period, while horizontal analysis compares the same item across periods; the two are usually used together. Percentages can hide scale, so always keep the absolute numbers in view.
example: Say ABC Ltd has revenue of ₹800 crore, raw material costs of ₹360 crore and employee costs of ₹96 crore. In a common-size income statement these become 100%, 45% (360 / 800) and 12% (96 / 800) of revenue.
formula: Common-size percentage = Line item / Base figure (revenue or total assets) x 100

short: Comparing the same items in a company's financial statements across several periods to see how much and how fast each one changed.
kid: Mark your height on the wall every birthday. Looking along all the marks shows how much you grew from one year to the next.
detail: Horizontal analysis compares line items in financial statements across two or more periods, either as absolute changes or percentage changes, and often against a base year set to 100. Reading across the columns of a multi-year profit and loss account or balance sheet shows which items are growing faster than revenue, for instance employee costs rising 25% while sales rise 10%, or receivables growing much faster than revenue, an early warning sign of collection trouble or aggressive accounting. It is the starting point for most company analysis and is how annual reports, research notes and screeners present five- or ten-year trends. Common confusion: horizontal analysis looks at change over time, whereas vertical analysis expresses items as a share of a base in a single period. Percentage changes from a very small base can look dramatic, and accounting changes such as the move to Ind AS can break comparability between years.
example: Say ABC Ltd's employee costs rose from ₹80 crore in FY24 to ₹100 crore in FY25, while revenue rose from ₹1,000 crore to ₹1,100 crore. Horizontal analysis shows employee costs up (100 - 80) / 80 = 25% against revenue up (1,100 - 1,000) / 1,000 = 10%, a squeeze on margins.
formula: Percentage change = (Current period amount - Base period amount) / Base period amount x 100

short: A formula that combines five financial ratios into one number to estimate how likely a company is to go bankrupt within about two years.
kid: A doctor checks your temperature, heartbeat and breathing, then says if you are healthy. This does the same check-up for a shop to see if it might get very sick.
detail: The Altman Z-score, published by economist Edward Altman in 1968, combines five weighted ratios to predict the likelihood of corporate bankruptcy. The original model for listed manufacturers uses working capital to total assets, retained earnings to total assets, EBIT to total assets, market value of equity to total liabilities, and sales to total assets. Scores above about 2.99 fall in the safe zone, 1.81 to 2.99 in the grey zone, and below 1.81 in the distress zone. Credit analysts, lenders and researchers use it as a quick screen for financial stress, including in Indian studies of stressed companies. Altman later published versions for private firms and for non-manufacturers and emerging markets, with different coefficients and cut-offs. Common confusion: the original model is not designed for banks, NBFCs or insurers, whose balance sheets work differently, and it is a screening tool, not a verdict.
example: Say a hypothetical ABC Ltd has the five ratios at 0.10, 0.20, 0.15, 1.00 and 1.20 in the order above. Its Z-score is 1.2(0.10) + 1.4(0.20) + 3.3(0.15) + 0.6(1.00) + 1.0(1.20) = 0.12 + 0.28 + 0.495 + 0.60 + 1.20 = 2.695, which falls in the grey zone.
formula: Z = 1.2 x (Working capital / Total assets) + 1.4 x (Retained earnings / Total assets) + 3.3 x (EBIT / Total assets) + 0.6 x (Market value of equity / Total liabilities) + 1.0 x (Sales / Total assets)

short: A score from 0 to 9 that rates a company's financial strength by awarding one point for each of nine simple health checks.
kid: Your teacher has nine little tests, and you get a star for each one you pass. More stars means you are doing really well.
detail: The Piotroski F-score, introduced by accounting professor Joseph Piotroski in a 2000 paper, awards one point for each of nine pass-or-fail tests across three areas. Profitability: positive net income, positive operating cash flow, rising return on assets, and operating cash flow exceeding net income. Leverage and liquidity: falling long-term debt ratio, rising current ratio, and no new shares issued. Operating efficiency: rising gross margin and rising asset turnover. Scores of 8 or 9 signal strength; Piotroski treated 0 or 1 as weak. Piotroski originally used it to separate winners from losers among cheap, high book-to-market stocks, and many Indian stock screeners now display it. Common confusion: the F-score measures year-on-year improvement in fundamentals, not valuation, so a high score does not mean a stock is cheap; it works best combined with a valuation filter. Banks and financial firms do not fit the tests well.
example: Say ABC Ltd passes the checks for positive profit, positive operating cash flow, cash flow above profit, lower debt, no new shares, better gross margin and higher asset turnover, but fails on improving return on assets and improving current ratio. It passes 7 of 9 tests, so its F-score is 7.
formula: F-score = Sum of 9 binary tests (1 if passed, 0 if not) across profitability, leverage and liquidity, and operating efficiency

short: Profit per share counted as if everyone holding a right to get new shares, such as employee stock options, had already used it.
kid: A pizza is cut for four friends, but two more friends were promised a slice. If you cut it for six instead, each slice is a bit smaller.
detail: Earnings per share (EPS) comes in two forms. Basic EPS divides profit attributable to equity shareholders by the weighted average number of shares outstanding during the period. Diluted EPS adds all potential shares that could be created from instruments such as employee stock options (ESOPs), warrants, convertible debentures and convertible preference shares, and adjusts profit for related items such as interest saved on convertibles. Only instruments that would reduce EPS, called dilutive ones, are included. Under Ind AS 33 and its global equivalent IAS 33, companies must present both figures in the statement of profit and loss. Diluted EPS is the more conservative figure and matters most for companies with large ESOP pools, such as new-age tech firms, or heavy convertible issuance. Common confusion: diluted EPS is never higher than basic EPS; if a calculation shows otherwise, an anti-dilutive instrument has been wrongly included.
example: Say ABC Ltd earns ₹100 crore with 50 crore shares outstanding, so basic EPS is 100 / 50 = ₹2. If employee options could add a net 5 crore shares, diluted EPS is 100 / 55 = about ₹1.82.
formula: Diluted EPS = (Profit attributable to equity shareholders + Adjustments for dilutive instruments) / (Weighted average shares + Dilutive potential shares)

short: A company's EBITDA, its profit before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, divided by tonnes sold, showing earnings on each tonne of cement or steel.
kid: A farmer sells big sacks of rice. This tells you how many coins the farmer really keeps from each sack after paying for seeds, water and helpers.
detail: EBITDA per tonne divides a company's EBITDA by its sales volume in tonnes. It is the headline profitability metric in commodity and bulk industries such as cement, steel, aluminium, zinc and fertilisers, because volumes are physical and prices move with the cycle. Indian brokerages routinely compare cement makers on EBITDA per tonne each quarter, since it strips out size differences and shows who earns more per unit through pricing power, cheaper fuel, captive power, logistics efficiency or a better product mix. Common confusion: companies may use different volume bases, such as sales versus production, or including or excluding traded volumes and clinker, and EBITDA may include or exclude other operating income and one-offs, so check definitions before comparing. It is a per-unit margin measure, so a company with lower EBITDA per tonne can still be more valuable if it grows volumes faster.
example: Say ABC Cement Ltd sells 10 million tonnes in a year and earns EBITDA of ₹1,000 crore. Since 10 million tonnes is 1 crore tonnes, its EBITDA per tonne is ₹1,000 crore / 1 crore tonnes = ₹1,000 per tonne.
formula: EBITDA per tonne = EBITDA / Sales volume in tonnes

short: The total gain an investor makes from owning a share over a period, counting both the price change and dividends received.
kid: You own a hen. Your prize is the eggs she lays plus how much more the hen is worth when she grows bigger.
detail: Total shareholder return (TSR) measures the full return to a shareholder over a period: share price appreciation plus dividends, usually assuming dividends are reinvested in the stock. It is the fairest way to compare investment performance across companies, because a high-dividend company and a high-growth company deliver returns in different forms. Boards increasingly link executive pay to TSR relative to peers, and consultancies publish TSR rankings. In India, total return indices (TRI) for benchmarks like the Nifty 50 apply the same idea, and SEBI has required mutual funds to benchmark against TRI rather than price-only indices since 2018. Common confusion: price return alone understates performance for dividend-paying stocks, roughly by the dividend yield each year; also, multi-year TSR should be annualised, like CAGR, before comparing periods of different lengths. For shareholders who do not sell into a buyback, its benefit shows up only through the share price.
example: Say you bought a share of ABC Ltd at ₹200, received ₹10 in dividends during the year and the price rose to ₹230. Your TSR is (230 - 200 + 10) / 200 = 20%, compared with a price return of only 30 / 200 = 15%.
formula: TSR = (Ending share price - Beginning share price + Dividends) / Beginning share price

short: The number of days a company could pay its running costs from cash and assets it can turn into cash quickly, if all income stopped.
kid: If your piggy bank stopped getting new coins, this counts how many days you could still buy your lunch with what is already inside.
detail: The defensive interval ratio (DIR) measures how many days a company can fund its operating expenses from its most liquid assets, namely cash, marketable securities and receivables, without relying on new revenue, borrowing or selling inventory. Daily operating expenses are usually taken as annual cash operating expenses, meaning total expenses excluding depreciation and other non-cash charges, divided by 365. Unlike the current and quick ratios, which compare liquid assets with liabilities at a point in time, DIR relates them to the ongoing cash burn, giving an intuitive survival horizon in days. It is especially useful for stress tests and for businesses facing a sudden revenue shock, as many did during the 2020 lockdowns. Common confusion: a long defensive interval is not automatically good, since excess idle cash can drag down returns; and the ratio ignores debt repayments falling due, so read it with the quick ratio and cash flow forecasts.
example: Say ABC Ltd holds cash of ₹30 crore, marketable securities of ₹20 crore and receivables of ₹40 crore, and its annual cash operating expenses are ₹365 crore, or ₹1 crore a day. Its defensive interval is (30 + 20 + 40) / 1 = 90 days.
formula: DIR (days) = (Cash + Marketable securities + Receivables) / Average daily cash operating expenses

short: Growth in the physical quantity a company sells, such as units, tonnes or litres, leaving out the effect of price changes.
kid: Your lemonade stand can earn more by selling more cups or by asking more for each cup. This only counts whether you sold more cups.
detail: Volume growth measures the change in the quantity of goods or services sold, in units, tonnes, litres or cases, separating it from price and mix effects. Revenue growth can be broken down into volume, price and mix, known as price-volume-mix analysis, and investors generally value volume-led growth more highly, because price hikes can hit a ceiling or reverse while rising volumes show genuine demand and market-share gains. Indian FMCG companies report underlying volume growth (UVG) or volume growth each quarter, and it is closely watched as a gauge of rural and urban consumption; automakers, cement and steel companies report monthly or quarterly dispatches. Common confusion: high revenue growth during inflation may hide flat or falling volumes, and a company can grow volumes while losing money if it is buying share through discounts. Definitions vary, for example in how acquisitions or certain categories are treated, so always read the footnote.
example: Say ABC Foods Ltd sold 100 crore packs at ₹10 last year and 104 crore packs at ₹10.50 this year. Revenue rose from ₹1,000 crore to ₹1,092 crore, or 9.2%, but volume growth was only 4%; the rest came from the 5% price increase.
formula: Volume growth = (Current period units sold - Prior period units sold) / Prior period units sold x 100
